page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 2 marks

steps.label: When Δn = 0
lines: If the number of moles of gaseous reactants
equals the number of moles of gaseous
products (Δn = 0), a change of pressure has
no effect on the equilibrium position.
steps.why: Pressure acts through the total number of gas moles. When both sides have the same number of gas moles, neither direction changes the volume, so pressure changes nothing.
common_mistakes: Claiming pressure always shifts a gaseous equilibrium. It does nothing when Δn = 0.
Counting solid or liquid substances in the moles. Only gaseous moles count.
steps.memory_tip: With the same number of gas moles on both sides, neither direction lowers the pressure, so the position does not shift.
steps.margin_note: State the Δn = 0 case first — it is the exception the examiner checks for.

steps.label: When Δn ≠ 0

lines.text: Increase of pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas moles

lines: Decrease of pressure shifts it towards the
equilibrium forward, because the right side
has 2 gas moles and the left side has 4.
steps.why: By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the applied change; fewer gas moles means lower pressure, so a pressure increase moves the reaction that way.
common_mistakes: Saying the shift goes towards more gas moles on a pressure increase — it is the opposite.
Giving no example. The ammonia equilibrium with its 4 and 2 gas moles is the expected one.
steps.memory_tip: Raise the pressure and the equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer gas moles, because fewer gas moles occupy less volume.
steps.margin_note: Count the gas moles on each side of the example and write both counts.

insider_note: Both cases are needed for full marks — the Δn = 0 case is the half most students leave out.
